strengths: The paper presents a clear and intuitively appealing two-stage framework: learn a task-agnostic policy representation using behavioral reconstruction, then optimize downstream policies in the learned latent space.
Using action agreement rather than weight reconstruction is well motivated because neural-network parameterizations contain substantial permutation and other functional redundancies.

The experiments examine multiple policy sizes, dataset sizes, and latent dimensions, and report results over multiple seeds with confidence intervals. The appendix provides architectures, training settings, baseline hyperparameters, and substantial additional visualization; supplementary code is also claimed to be available.
The finding that latent-space PGPE can optimize policies much more effectively than parameter-space PGPE is promising, particularly for parameter-based exploration methods.
weaknesses: The central claim that the intrinsic dimension is determined by environmental complexity rather than network size is not convincingly established. Only two relatively simple environments are studied, there is no estimator of intrinsic dimension, and the reported task-return recovery does not demonstrate coverage of the behavioral manifold. Indeed, the paper observes that larger policies produce richer and more readily recovered representations.

The behavioral objective is only an action-space MSE over an externally constructed set of states—gridded states in Mountain Car and uniformly sampled bounded states in Reacher. This is not the stated divergence between state-action occupancy distributions, may heavily weight unreachable states, and does not justify the claimed connection to behavior. The cited upper-bound intuition is especially questionable for deterministic policies and an unweighted Euclidean action metric.

The formal compression criterion in Eq. 4 requires every policy in the full parameter space to have a behaviorally equivalent latent code, but neither the finite dataset procedure nor the experiments support this universal condition. A continuous decoder from a 1–3 dimensional space cannot generally cover all behaviors of an unrestricted high-dimensional policy class without much stronger structural assumptions.

The principal compression evidence is weak. The reported 'performance recovery' compares extrema under four hand-designed reward functions, uses a normalization involving dataset lower bounds, and can exceed one. It neither measures held-out behavioral reconstruction nor establishes preservation of policy-class expressivity. Consequently, the advertised 121,801:1 compression ratio is largely the ratio of parameter count to latent-code dimension, not evidence of equivalent behavioral capacity.

The downstream comparison does not isolate the value of the proposed components. Important baselines and ablations are missing, including a weight-reconstruction autoencoder, no novelty filtering, alternative state sampling, random projections or random latent decoders, direct optimization of an equally small policy, and related skill-discovery or policy-manifold approaches. Baseline network sizes are selected by best performance, while the latent method benefits from a separately learned decoder and policy corpus.

Claims of improved sample efficiency count only downstream environment steps and omit the potentially substantial pretraining and dataset-construction cost. Even if policy generation uses no rollouts, the method assumes access to state-space bounds and evaluates up to 100,000 policies over thousands of chosen states; its computational and memory scaling are not compared with baselines.

The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad DRL and multi-task claims: Mountain Car is very small, Reacher uses short 50-step episodes and artificial velocity rewards, and no standard URL benchmark, higher-dimensional locomotion problem, image observation setting, or transfer across environments is tested. One of eight downstream tasks fails because the required behavior is absent from the dataset, exposing a fundamental coverage limitation.

Statistical support for the downstream conclusions is incomplete: there are no final-performance or sample-to-threshold tables, significance tests, or robustness studies, and the statement that convergence is faster on seven of eight tasks is inferred from noisy learning curves. Some experimental definitions are also unclear or apparently erroneous, such as the Reacher clockwise threshold reported as tangential velocity greater than -11.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3664177726374eeb8b673abbff0591ad/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} proposes a coherent and potentially useful two-stage framework: behavior-aware policy compression followed by downstream optimization in the learned latent space.

The behavioral reconstruction objective is intuitive and better aligned with functional policy similarity than direct reconstruction of neural-network weights. The paper also clearly acknowledges that downstream success depends on coverage of the policy dataset.

The presentation is generally readable, and the appendix supplies architectures, hyperparameters, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and many latent-space visualizations. The experiments show that latent-space PGPE can be effective on several of the studied tasks.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-dimensionality claim is not established. The paper performs no intrinsic-dimension estimation and provides no controlled evidence that dimension depends on environmental complexity rather than policy size. Results from only two simple environments and a few hand-selected latent dimensions cannot support this broad conclusion.

The evaluation lacks essential baselines and ablations: parameter-reconstruction autoencoders or VAEs, PCA/random subspaces, direct optimization of equivalently small policies, behavior-vector representations, and ablations of novelty filtering and the behavioral loss. Consequently, it is unclear which component produces the reported gains or whether the proposed method is superior to much simpler alternatives.

The method does not actually reconstruct the defined state-action occupancy distributions. It compares deterministic actions on a fixed set of uniformly sampled states. In Reacher, uniform sampling of sine and cosine coordinates can produce physically invalid states, so the loss may emphasize behavior outside the reachable state distribution. This substantially weakens the connection between the formal objective and implementation.

The reported performance-recovery metric compares extrema over a discretized latent grid with extrema in the source dataset. It neither measures held-out behavioral reconstruction nor coverage, and it is sensitive to the number and placement of evaluated grid points. Values above one therefore do not convincingly demonstrate preservation or improvement of expressivity. Quantitative compression results are also largely limited to Mountain Car.

The downstream sample-efficiency comparison excludes the substantial policy-generation, novelty-selection, and autoencoder-training stages. Even if this cost can be amortized across tasks, the paper provides no end-to-end accounting, break-even analysis, or scaling study. Comparisons against task-trained RL baselines based only on fine-tuning timesteps therefore overstate the efficiency conclusion.

The claimed 121,801:1 compression rate counts only latent coordinates and ignores the shared decoder, whose input/output layers can contain millions of parameters, as well as the policy archive and training cost. This ratio is potentially misleading unless explicitly presented as amortized per-policy code storage.

The experimental scope is too narrow for the claims: Mountain Car is very simple, Reacher is modified into short-horizon threshold-reward tasks, and one Mountain Car task fails because the archive lacks the required behavior. Baseline tuning is also not persuasive—Reacher largely reuses Mountain Car hyperparameters—and the main Reacher plots omit weaker baselines.

Several technical and reproducibility details remain problematic. Equation 4 is not a well-formed global optimization objective; the parameter-sampling distribution and its bounds are insufficiently specified; and the main text's ten-run reporting is difficult to reconcile with the appendix's description of 75 runs on 75 autoencoders. Overall, the idea is plausible, but the evidence does not substantiate its strongest claims or make it competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and appealing framework: construct a behaviorally organized latent policy space without task rewards, then perform downstream policy search in this substantially lower-dimensional space.

The behavioral reconstruction loss is a meaningful improvement over parameter-space reconstruction because it accounts for the many-to-one relationship between neural-network parameters and policy functions.
The empirical study is reasonably broad within the selected domains, varying policy size, dataset size, and latent dimension, and reporting multiple seeds and confidence intervals.

Latent PGPE achieves encouraging downstream results, often learning faster than conventional PGPE and several standard deep-RL baselines. The failure on the Mountain Car height task is also discussed candidly.
The paper is generally well organized, provides extensive implementation details and visualizations, and states that source code is included in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-dimensionality claim is not convincingly established. No intrinsic-dimension estimator or formal analysis is provided; successful task returns from one- to eight-dimensional embeddings in only two relatively simple environments do not demonstrate that dimension depends on environment complexity rather than network size.

The reported compression ratio is potentially misleading. A 121,801-dimensional policy is represented by a one-dimensional code only when accompanied by a learned decoder whose parameter count can exceed that of the original policy. The result demonstrates low-dimensional optimization coordinates, not an equivalent reduction in total storage or model complexity.

The formal objective concerns state-action occupancy distributions and all policies in the parameter space, whereas the implemented loss compares actions on a finite, largely uniformly sampled state set and only for sampled policies. This proxy can overweight unreachable states, ignores induced state visitation, and offers no demonstrated guarantee of occupancy reconstruction.

Compression quality is evaluated mainly through a task-dependent performance-recovery statistic based on extrema over a discretized latent space. This can remain high while most training policies or behavioral modes are reconstructed poorly. Held-out per-policy behavioral error, occupancy divergence, coverage metrics, and comparisons against parameter-reconstruction autoencoders are needed.

The downstream sample-efficiency comparison excludes the potentially substantial cost of generating, filtering, and training on up to 100,000 policies. Amortizing this cost across tasks is reasonable, but the paper should report it explicitly and show break-even performance as the number of downstream tasks changes.

The baseline set does not include the most relevant latent-policy, quality-diversity, or unsupervised-RL alternatives discussed in the related work. Baseline tuning and initialization details are also insufficient to rule out an advantage from representation or hyperparameter selection.

Generalization evidence is narrow: experiments cover only Mountain Car and Reacher, use low-dimensional state/action spaces and hand-designed related tasks, and do not test whether the learned manifold transfers across dynamics, policy architectures, or substantially more complex control domains.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and intuitively appealing framework: construct a diverse policy dataset, learn a low-dimensional decoder using action-level behavioral reconstruction, and optimize downstream policies in the resulting latent space.

Using functional outputs rather than weight reconstruction is a sensible way to reduce sensitivity to neural-network parameter symmetries, and differentiability of the decoder permits several latent-space optimization strategies.

The empirical study spans four continuous-control environments, multiple policy and latent dimensions, several dataset sizes, and multiple seeds. The appendix provides substantial implementation and hyperparameter detail.

The results indicate that latent PGPE can substantially outperform parameter-space PGPE and can learn some Mountain Car and Reacher tasks with fewer downstream interactions than standard deep-RL baselines.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-dimension claim is not established. The paper does not estimate manifold dimension or compare controlled behavior classes across network sizes; showing that selected rewards can be recovered from small latent codes is insufficient to conclude that dimensionality is determined by environment complexity rather than policy parameterization.

The claimed behavioral loss is only an action discrepancy on roughly 3,000 uniformly sampled states inside hand-selected bounds. It neither measures the stated state-action occupancy divergence nor emphasizes reachable or policy-induced states. In MuJoCo, uniform samples in a bounding box can be physically invalid, substantially weakening the interpretation as behavior preservation.

The sample-efficiency comparison excludes the large pretraining expense: generation and novelty filtering of up to 100,000 policies, state evaluations, and autoencoder training. No amortization analysis identifies how many downstream tasks are required to recover this cost, so claims of addressing DRL sample inefficiency are overstated.

The performance-recovery metric is based on extrema and ranges of randomly generated datasets, can exceed one, becomes unstable when the dataset range is small, and does not measure reconstruction coverage or expected behavioral fidelity. Consequently, it provides weak evidence that most of the original policy space's expressivity is retained.

Downstream optimization is evaluated only on Mountain Car and Reacher, while Hopper and HalfCheetah appear only in the indirect recovery analysis. Thus the practical fine-tuning claims are not demonstrated in the more challenging domains.

Several downstream rewards are narrow or potentially problematic proxies. In particular, the stated Reacher clockwise condition uses tangential velocity greater than -11, whereas counterclockwise uses greater than 1; this does not define symmetric opposing behaviors and may make the former task unusually easy. Results depend heavily on these custom tasks.

Important ablations are missing, including parameter-reconstruction autoencoders, unfiltered random policy datasets, reachable-state sampling, alternative behavioral metrics, direct random search in latent space, and modern unsupervised or skill-learning approaches. It is therefore unclear which component produces the reported gains.

The formal compression objective is imprecisely written and supplies no guarantee that a single low-dimensional generator approximates all policies. The paper moves from this idealized occupancy-level objective to a materially different empirical surrogate without analyzing the approximation gap.

The main conclusions are stronger than the evidence: performance is sometimes poor or highly variable, the height task fails, some confidence intervals are very wide, and only three seeds are used for much of the key Mountain Car compression study. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evaluation does not adequately substantiate its headline claims for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive, modular idea: learn a task-agnostic latent policy space using action-level reconstruction, then optimize downstream policies through the frozen decoder. Avoiding parameter-space symmetries through functional reconstruction is sensible.

The empirical study covers four continuous-control environments, several network and latent-space sizes, and multiple downstream rewards. The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, hyperparameters, compute requirements, and additional visualizations.
The comparison between parameter-space PGPE and latent PGPE illustrates a plausible practical benefit of reducing the search dimension, and several downstream learning curves are promising.

The manuscript is generally well organized, explicitly states its research questions, discusses relevant weight-space and policy-manifold literature, and acknowledges that downstream performance is constrained by coverage of the pretraining dataset.
weaknesses: The central sample-efficiency claim is not established. Downstream curves exclude the potentially substantial cost of generating and filtering up to 100,000 policies, evaluating them on thousands of states, and training the autoencoder. Latent PGPE therefore receives extensive pretraining that is not accounted for in comparisons with methods trained from scratch.

The implemented loss does not faithfully measure the state-action occupancy divergence used in the formulation. It compares deterministic actions on roughly 3,000 manually bounded, uniformly sampled states. In high-dimensional MuJoCo domains these samples will overwhelmingly be off the reachable-state distribution, and action agreement there neither guarantees similar visitation distributions nor behavioral equivalence under the environment dynamics. The cited divergence bound does not by itself justify this particular finite-state L2 proxy.

The reported compression ratio is misleading. It compares the latent-code dimension with the parameter count of one policy while ignoring the shared decoder, whose input/output layers scale with the original policy size. This may provide an amortized representation of many policies, but it is not a five-orders-of-magnitude compression of the complete model.

The performance-recovery metric is a task-dependent comparison of extrema rather than a direct reconstruction or coverage measure. It compares the best of as many as 10,000 decoded samples with the best policy in a differently sized dataset, after normalizing by empirical reward ranges. Values above one can arise from extreme-value sampling and evaluation noise and do not demonstrate preservation of the original policy space's expressivity. Held-out behavioral reconstruction errors, coverage/precision measures, and matched-sample comparisons are missing.

The main intrinsic-dimension hypothesis is not convincingly tested. The paper does not estimate intrinsic dimension or identify a reconstruction-versus-dimension threshold, and environment complexity, policy architecture, random-weight behavior distribution, and dataset coverage are confounded. Showing that some task rewards can be recovered from 1–16 latent variables is insufficient to conclude that behavioral dimensionality is largely network-size invariant.

Essential ablations and comparisons are absent: parameter-reconstruction autoencoders, PCA or random projections, unfiltered random-policy datasets, alternative state sampling schemes, direct optimization of genuinely small policies, and closely related policy-manifold or generative-policy methods. Consequently, it is unclear which gains arise from behavioral reconstruction, novelty filtering, decoder-induced priors, or simply low-dimensional PGPE.

The downstream evidence is narrow and uneven. Fine-tuning is evaluated only on Mountain Car and Reacher, despite compression results on Hopper and HalfCheetah; several rewards are hand-designed threshold objectives, and the Reacher horizon is only 50 steps. Baselines largely use defaults or limited manual modifications, whereas the proposed method is evaluated with selected configurations, and some weak baselines are omitted from the main figure.

Statistical support is incomplete. Mountain Car compression results use only three seeds, claims such as statistically significant generalization and faster convergence in seven of eight tasks are made without formal tests, and the appendix's description of 75 seeded PGPE runs is difficult to reconcile with figures described as averages over 10 runs.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evaluation does not support the strongest claims about behavior-space compression, intrinsic dimensionality, or improved DRL sample efficiency. These are central rather than cosmetic deficiencies, placing the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and interesting contribution: learning a low-dimensional policy search space using a behavior-level reconstruction objective, then performing task-specific optimization directly in that space.
The behavioral reconstruction loss is well motivated by neural-network parameter symmetries and is more appropriate than raw weight reconstruction for grouping functionally similar policies.

The experiments cover four continuous-control environments, multiple network and dataset sizes, several latent dimensions, and multiple random seeds. Results show substantial dimensionality reduction while retaining useful policies.
The downstream Latent PGPE experiments provide concrete evidence of practical value: the learned space often enables much faster optimization than parameter-space PGPE and standard deep-RL baselines.
The method is modular, conceptually simple, and potentially useful beyond the particular autoencoder and PGPE instantiations studied here.
The presentation is generally clear, with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, uncertainty estimates, and additional visualizations supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—that behavioral-manifold dimensionality is governed by environment complexity rather than network size—is not established convincingly. Recovering performance extrema on four hand-designed rewards does not demonstrate preservation of the full behavior manifold or measure its intrinsic dimension.

The central behavioral loss is not adequately ablated. In particular, the paper lacks comparisons against parameter-reconstruction autoencoders, unfiltered random policy datasets, alternative state-sampling schemes, and other policy-representation or generative-policy approaches. These comparisons are important for identifying which component produces the gains.

Action agreement is measured on roughly 3,000 uniformly sampled states from manually bounded boxes. Many such states may be unreachable, while behavior was formally defined through occupancy distributions. The paper does not quantify how well this proxy correlates with actual state-action occupancy divergence.

The reported compression ratio counts only the latent-code dimension relative to policy parameters. The decoder must still be stored and evaluated and can itself be large, so this is primarily search-space dimensionality reduction rather than model-size compression; the terminology and claims should be qualified.

Downstream sample-efficiency curves exclude the substantial one-time cost of constructing policy datasets and training the representation. Amortization across tasks is plausible, but the paper does not provide an end-to-end compute or sample accounting or determine how many downstream tasks are needed to offset pretraining.

Fine-tuning is evaluated only on Mountain Car and Reacher, using custom tasks that often favor broad behavioral exploration. Hopper and HalfCheetah are evaluated only through recovery statistics, limiting evidence that the optimization gains scale to harder control problems.

Comparisons are mainly against task-specific RL trained from scratch. A stronger evaluation would compare with unsupervised-RL, skill-discovery, or other pretrained policy-space methods under matched pretraining and fine-tuning budgets. Some baseline tuning and run-count descriptions are also insufficiently transparent for a definitive fairness assessment.
